title: Checking and Shaping Output
description: Catching hallucinations and bias, checking sources and claims, and choosing inline, artifact or file output.

cards.definition: Claude producing incorrect or misleading information that can sound confident and authoritative but has no basis, which is why factual claims need checking.
Prompting tricks reduce hallucinations but never remove them, so critical facts still need independent validation, especially for high-stakes decisions.
A prompt technique that explicitly lets Claude admit uncertainty or missing information, which can sharply cut made-up answers.
For long documents, have Claude first pull out word-for-word quotes, then base its analysis only on those quotes.
Asking Claude to find a supporting quote for each claim in a draft and remove any claim it cannot support.
Run the same prompt several times and compare the answers; inconsistencies between runs can signal a hallucination.
A general follow-up asking Claude to re-check or expand its earlier answer, which can surface and fix inconsistencies.
Telling Claude to answer only from the material you supplied, not its general knowledge; no quotes required.
With web search on, answers link to the sources used; cross-check them and rely on authoritative sources for important decisions.
In a doc or Markdown artifact, highlight a passage to have Claude revise just that section instead of the whole piece.
Define the exact structure you want, such as JSON, XML, or a template, so Claude follows every formatting element consistently.
Claude's mistakes can read as polished and plausible while being badly wrong, so a fluent, confident tone is not evidence that content is accurate.
Anthropic research found models judge their own answers well on familiar tasks but poorly on unfamiliar ones, so confident wording is not proof.
Claude can produce quotes that look authoritative but have no basis in the source, so check any quoted wording against the original before you use it.
Claude's synthesis can leave out context that changes a source's meaning, and answers are only as good as the sources behind them, so open the cited pages.
Each model has a knowledge cutoff and may not know later events, so verify dates, prices, and recent developments against current sources.
Anthropic tests balance by sending the same contested request from opposing viewpoints and comparing depth, counterarguments, and refusals; you can run similar paired prompts.
Anthropic says its political even-handedness measures are imperfect: no agreed definition of bias exists, and results can vary between runs, so review sensitive content yourself.
Claude uses an artifact for significant, self-contained content, typically over 15 lines, that you will edit, reuse, or share; short conversational answers stay inline.
Pick the output type by use: Excel for formulas and charts, Word or PDF for reports with analysis, PowerPoint for decks, instead of copying chat text by hand.
Generated files may need refining to meet exact requirements, so state the structure, content, and formatting you want and check the result before sharing.
Editing an earlier message creates a separate branch with its own artifacts, letting you compare a different direction without losing the first version.
